title: A 10-Second Video of Your Eyes Can Now Detect Iron Deficiency Without a Blood Test. South Asian Women Should Be Paying Attention.
excerpt: Israeli researchers built a needle-free test that spots anaemia by analysing blood vessels in the whites of your eyes. For a community where half of all women are iron-deficient, this could change how millions get screened.
body:
Iron deficiency anaemia is one of the most common nutritional disorders on earth. It is also one of the most underdiagnosed. Roughly 1.6 billion people worldwide are affected, and the standard way to detect it — a blood draw sent to a laboratory — remains inaccessible to hundreds of millions, particularly in low-income settings and immigrant communities where routine bloodwork often falls through the cracks.

A new study now suggests there may be a far simpler way to find it. Researchers in Israel have developed a technique that detects anaemia by recording a 10-second video of the whites of a person's eyes.

## How the Test Works

The method analyses the network of tiny blood vessels visible in the conjunctiva — the thin, transparent membrane covering the white part of the eye. In a healthy individual, these vessels carry oxygen-rich, haemoglobin-dense red blood cells that give them a characteristic colour. In someone who is anaemic, the reduced haemoglobin alters the visual signature of those vessels in ways that are subtle to the human eye but detectable by a camera and an algorithm.

In a trial involving 224 participants, the needle-free technique correctly identified anaemia in more than 80 per cent of cases. The researchers say the test is not yet ready to replace laboratory blood work, but it could dramatically simplify the process of initial screening — particularly in settings where access to laboratories is scarce.

"It's great research but will take a lot of steps to be clinically available," said Dr Peter Campbell, an ophthalmologist at Oregon Health & Science University, who was not involved in the study.

## Why This Matters for South Asian Families

Iron deficiency anaemia is not distributed evenly. According to the World Health Organization, South Asia has among the highest prevalence rates on the planet. In India alone, roughly 53 per cent of women of reproductive age are anaemic. Among pregnant women, the figure is even higher. The condition contributes to fatigue, cognitive impairment, poor pregnancy outcomes, and increased vulnerability to infection.

For South Asian families in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Canada, the problem persists — though the reasons shift. Vegetarian and vegan diets, which are common in Hindu, Jain, and Buddhist households, provide non-haeme iron that the body absorbs less efficiently than the haeme iron found in meat. Tea consumed with meals, a cultural staple, contains tannins that further inhibit iron absorption. Many women in the diaspora go years without a comprehensive blood panel, particularly if they lack insurance or are between primary care providers.

The result is a large population carrying undiagnosed iron deficiency that manifests as chronic fatigue, difficulty concentrating, shortness of breath, and hair loss — symptoms that are often dismissed as stress or ageing.

## The Smartphone Possibility

What makes this research particularly compelling is the potential for smartphone deployment. A 10-second video of someone's eye is something any modern phone camera can capture. If the algorithm can be packaged into a mobile application, it could enable mass screening without needles, labs, or appointments.

That kind of accessibility matters most in the communities where anaemia is most prevalent. A woman in suburban New Jersey who has been meaning to get bloodwork for two years but has not found the time could screen herself at home. A college student in London whose vegetarian diet is leaving her perpetually exhausted could get a signal that something is wrong before it affects her academic performance. A grandmother in Hyderabad who has never had a formal blood test could be screened by a community health worker carrying nothing more than a phone.

## What This Does Not Do

The test is not a diagnosis. An 80 per cent detection rate means one in five anaemic individuals would be missed, and the study's sample size of 224 is small by clinical standards. Before any smartphone application could be approved for medical use, it would need to demonstrate accuracy across diverse skin tones, lighting conditions, and age groups — all factors that could affect the visibility of conjunctival vessels.

The researchers have also not yet published data on false positives — healthy individuals incorrectly flagged as anaemic. A high false-positive rate could generate unnecessary anxiety and medical visits, partially offsetting the convenience benefit.

## The Broader Pattern

This study is part of a larger trend in point-of-care diagnostics: using cameras, sensors, and machine learning to bring screening out of the laboratory and into the home. Smartphone-based tests for skin cancer, heart rhythm abnormalities, and respiratory conditions are already in various stages of development and regulatory review.

For iron deficiency anaemia — a condition that is common, consequential, and disproportionately prevalent in South Asian populations — a needle-free, phone-based screening tool would be more than a technological novelty. It would be a public health intervention aimed squarely at the people who need it most.

The science is not yet there. But the direction is clear. And for the millions of South Asian women living with undiagnosed iron deficiency, even a partial solution is better than the silence that currently passes for screening.
